subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If the expression (x − p)/(x² − 3x + 2) takes all real values for x ∈ R, then find the bounds for p.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.54 (PDF p.55 — in this region of the scan the offset is book + 1, not the book + 2 that docs/IPE_MATHS_2A_SOURCE.md states; the page number printed on the page is the authority) — SAQ chapter 8 Quadratic Expressions, answer 67. Truth-check: the book's open interval 1 < p < 2 is correct — at p = 1 the expression reduces to 1/(x − 2), which never equals 0, and at p = 2 to 1/(x − 1), likewise; so neither end value lets the expression take all real values. Also checked: x = 1 and x = 2 (the excluded points) are never roots of the quadratic in x when 1 < p < 2 (substituting gives p − 1 and p − 2), so the discriminant argument introduces nothing false.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the bounds for p — say what you call y, what quadratic in x you form, what x being real gives, why that inequality must hold for every y, what condition on p that gives, and why the two end values are left out.
insider_note: 'Takes all real values' turns the second discriminant condition into ≤ 0 — true for every y, not for some y. And the end values of p are excluded with a written reason: there the numerator cancels a factor of the denominator, so the bounds are strict.

steps.label: Quadratic in x
steps.margin_note: First mark. The x terms collect to −(3y + 1)x and the constant is 2y + p. The denominator is (x − 1)(x − 2), so x = 1 and x = 2 are excluded; neither is a root of (1) for the p found later, so nothing false enters.
lines: (1) is a quadratic in x, and x is real.

recall.must_convey: That the expression is set equal to y, cross-multiplied, and collected into a quadratic in x: yx² − (3y + 1)x + (2y + p) = 0.
accept: let y equal the expression, cross multiply and collect terms to get a quadratic in x
put y equal to the fraction, multiply out the denominator and write it as a quadratic in x
call the expression y and rearrange it into a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero
expression ni y ani pettukoni cross multiply chesi x lo quadratic rayali

steps.why: The question is about which y are possible; writing the fraction as a quadratic in x is what lets the discriminant answer that.
common_mistakes: Dropping the p when moving x − p across.
Not writing that (1) is a quadratic in x with x real.

steps.label: Δ ≥ 0
steps.margin_note: Second mark. a = y, b = −(3y + 1), c = 2y + p. 4ac = 8y² + 4py. Collect the y terms: 6y − 4py = (6 − 4p)y. Label it (2) — the next step reasons about it.

recall.must_convey: That x real gives Δ ≥ 0: (3y + 1)² − 4y(2y + p) ≥ 0, which simplifies to y² + (6 − 4p)y + 1 ≥ 0, a quadratic in y whose middle coefficient contains p.
accept: x is real so the discriminant b squared minus four a c must be greater than or equal to zero
the quadratic in x has real roots so delta is at least zero
apply b squared minus 4 a c greater than or equal to zero to the quadratic in x
x real kabatti delta greater than or equal to zero pettali
heard_as: b squared minus four a c
greater than or equal to zero

steps.why: This inequality says which y the expression can take, for a given p. The question turns it around: p must be such that EVERY real y satisfies it.
common_mistakes: Using Δ > 0, which changes the later condition on p.

steps.label: Condition on p
steps.margin_note: Third mark, and the idea of the question. 'Takes all real values' means (2) is true for EVERY y. A quadratic in y with positive leading coefficient stays ≥ 0 everywhere only if it never goes below the axis — its own discriminant must be ≤ 0. Note the direction: ≤, not ≥.
lines: y takes all real values, so (2) holds
The coefficient of y² is 1 > 0, so (2)
holds for all y only if its Δ ≤ 0:

recall.must_convey: That because the expression takes ALL real values, inequality (2) must hold for every y; with leading coefficient positive that needs the discriminant of (2) to be ≤ 0, giving (6 − 4p)² − 4 ≤ 0 and hence 1 ≤ p ≤ 2.
accept: since y takes all real values the inequality must hold for every y so the discriminant of the quadratic in y must be less than or equal to zero
the quadratic in y has positive leading coefficient so it is always non negative only if its discriminant is at most zero which gives p between one and two
apply the discriminant condition a second time, this time to the quadratic in y, with less than or equal to zero
y anni values teeskuntundi kabatti y lo quadratic ki discriminant less than or equal to zero pettali, p one ki two ki madhya vasthundi
six minus four p squared minus four is at most zero so p is between one and two
heard_as: less than or equal to zero

steps.why: A quadratic that opens upward is ≥ 0 for every input exactly when it has no two distinct real roots, i.e. its discriminant is ≤ 0. That is the second, and decisive, use of the discriminant in this question.
common_mistakes: Using Δ ≥ 0 again by habit — for 'true for all y' the condition is Δ ≤ 0.

steps.label: Bounds for p
steps.margin_note: Last mark, and where most answers stop early. At p = 1 the numerator (x − 1) cancels a factor of the denominator and the expression becomes 1/(x − 2), which never takes the value 0; at p = 2 it becomes 1/(x − 1), likewise. So the end values are excluded and the bounds are strict.
lines: If p = 1 or p = 2, the numerator cancels
expression no longer takes all real values.
So p = 1 and p = 2 are not allowed.

recall.must_convey: That p = 1 and p = 2 must be rejected because the numerator then cancels a factor of the denominator and the expression stops taking all real values, so the bounds are 1 < p < 2, strict.
accept: p equal to one or two makes the numerator cancel with the denominator so those are left out and the answer is p strictly between one and two
at the end values the fraction reduces to one over x minus two or one over x minus one which never gives zero so exclude them
reject p equals one and p equals two, so one less than p less than two
p one leda two aithe numerator denominator tho cancel avthundi, so strict inequality one less than p less than two
the bounds are one and two but not including them
reject: p is between one and two

steps.why: The inequality on p came from the discriminant of (1), which assumed the fraction was really a quadratic problem. When numerator and denominator share a factor the fraction is a different, simpler function, and the assumption fails — so the two end values have to be tested separately and thrown out.
common_mistakes: Answering 1 ≤ p ≤ 2 with the ends included.
Giving no reason for excluding p = 1 and p = 2.
Excluding only one of the two end values.
